title: When Checklists Backfire at Equalized Budgets: Dissecting Static Chain-of-Thought Prefills and Budget Starvation in Mechatronic Control and Fault Diagnosis
content: Static chain-of-thought (CoT) prefills, such as domain checklists injected at the start of a model's reasoning, are a popular training-free way to steer compact language models on engineering tasks. Our earlier 900-token experiments on mechatronic control and fault diagnosis suggested that such a prefill helped a distilled reasoning model. A re-audit showed that the vanilla arm was truncated on most items at that budget and the prefill mainly reduced truncation. We therefore ran a pre-registered, budget-controlled replication (protocol v2.0, frozen before any GPU job). Four open-weight 7B-8B models received three problem-agnostic assistant-turn prefills (a physical checklist, a generic step-wise checklist, and domain keywords only) at an equalized 4096-token budget, and were compared with a byte-identical, parity-verified no-prefill control arm. In total we analyse 6,400 trajectories on MechaCoT-400. All are graded by a deterministic verifier that requires a strict final decision line and compiles and simulates IEC 61131-3 Structured Text with the RuSTy compiler. On the primary scope (Clean-370: 185 counterfactual pairs, 19 archetype clusters), the physical checklist did not improve pair-consistent decision accuracy. It lowered it, from 165/370 (44.59%) to 132/370 (35.68%): Δ = -8.92 pp, exact McNemar p_Holm = 0.0270, which is a significant decrease under the pre-registered rule. Because the 370 paired instances span 19 archetype clusters across two models, we also report cluster-level inference: the archetype-clustered BCa interval is [-18.18, +0.27] pp and an exact paired cluster sign-flip test across the 19 clusters (under a cluster-wise sign-symmetry assumption) gives p = 0.0979. Both item-pair and cluster-level bounds lie well below the pre-registered +3.0 pp minimum practical benefit threshold, ruling out a meaningful gain while leaving cluster-level uncertainty on the harm magnitude in the two-model pool. The domain-anchor contrast (H2, Δ = -5.68 pp) and the structure-versus-vocabulary contrast (H3, Δ = -6.49 pp) are inconclusive. In an exploratory pool of all four models, the decrease is consistent in sign across every model and significant at both item-pair and cluster levels: Δ = -9.05 pp, p_Holm = 1.80e-4, BCa [-14.40, -4.31] pp, cluster sign-flip p = 0.0052. The decrease persists in pairs where no arm was truncated, and it occurs in a model that is essentially never truncated. Truncation therefore does not explain it. Executable correctness is low throughout: no open-weight arm passes more than 8.18% of the RuSTy behavioural testbenches. Static domain checklists do not improve pair-consistent decisions once output budgets and answer formats are equalized; the earlier 900-token gains were attributable to reduced truncation.
